requirements.requirement: Explain how spatial methods retain tissue location while protein and RNA assays measure different molecules.
Keep one thin tissue section distinct from the whole tumour and from loss of spatial context in a ground-up sample.
Assess the claim that every spatial method requires cell segmentation; distinguish cell-assigned results from pooled regions or capture spots.
Treat the sampled tissue section as finite and account for assay use of material.
Keep observed neighbours separate from evidence of biological interaction.
Distinguish antibody-tagged protein detection by repeated fluorescence cycles from metal-tag detection by mass.
Explain why a question about a drug target on particular cells needs an appropriate protein measurement and cellular assignment.
Require marker-specific antibody validation and qualify panel size as a method-specific constraint.
Distinguish RNA detection using probes or barcoded capture from antibody protein detection and describe broad gene panels.
Keep transcription separate from protein abundance and cell-surface localisation.
Preserve the diagram's two independent choices: molecular layer and chosen regions versus the imaged area.
Describe digital spatial profiling as tag counts from selected tissue areas rather than a map of individual cells.
Verify Merritt's region sizes of one to about 5,000 cells and panels of 44 proteins or 1,412 genes, with method-paper scope.
Explain pooled regional results and dependence on who selected the regions and why.
Distinguish mapping the complete imaged field from assuming that the entire slide or tumour was measured.
Verify Lin's example of up to 60 protein markers on formalin-fixed sections using standard microscopes.
Verify Giesen's 32-protein breast-cancer imaging example, subcellular resolution and destruction of the sampled area by laser ablation.
Verify Keren's ion-beam example of 36 proteins in 41 triple-negative breast tumours.
Describe Ståhl's sequencing-based transcriptome capture in human breast cancer, retaining capture-spot mixtures rather than assuming single cells.
Verify Chen's 100-to-1,000-gene imaging example, individual RNA molecules and assignment to cells, with a targeted panel.
Keep all cited panel sizes historical and require the actual study method rather than treating them as current platform limits.
Verify the mixed versus compartmentalised immune patterns and survival association in Keren's 41-tumour cohort without turning it into a treatment test.
Explain when broad RNA mapping supports discovery of cell states and pathways before choosing markers.
Choose predefined regional profiling for known compartments and mapped imaging for borders, neighbourhoods or rare-cell questions.
Carry the analogy's underlying distinction between measured proteins, measured transcripts, chosen samples and spatial maps without treating the analogy as biology.
Explain why regional readouts and multicellular capture spots make spatial measurement different from universal single-cell resolution.
Carry the fictional 40-marker versus six-marker comparison: including the relevant target can matter more than panel size.
Require protein verification for a targeting question despite detected RNA.
Do not infer cell interaction or functional engagement merely from spatial adjacency.
Distinguish cited research multiplex methods from validated clinical receptor or PD-L1 immunohistochemistry without making an exhaustive regulatory claim.
For one spare section and a target-near-T-cells question, specify protein detection for the target, cancer cells and T cells over an appropriate imaged area.
Explain why regional RNA would not answer which cells carry that protein in the exercise.
Answer the teach-back choice among protein, RNA and predefined regional profiling using the question, measured molecule and sampling design.
Define spatial proximity metrics as relationships in a cell map and distinguish them from density, with a single two-dimensional section as the sampled object.
Specify cell type and x-y coordinates as inputs, with image segmentation and cell typing as sources of error.
Define compartment density with its cell-count denominator and tumour-epithelium or stromal area, for example CD8 cells per square millimetre.
Define a radius count and fraction with the reference cell population and distance threshold stated.
Define directed nearest-neighbour distance, including a summary such as the median from each T cell to the closest cancer cell.
Define the directed cross-type nearest-neighbour distribution G-cross across radii and distinguish a curve or its 0-to-20-micrometre area from a single fixed-radius fraction.
Verify the immune-tumour versus immune-immune contact ratio used as a mixing-score example.
Treat Morisita-Horn colocalisation as a separate spatial abundance metric rather than assuming all mixing scores share one definition.
Explain recurring cellular neighbourhoods using the example of clustering each cell's ten nearest neighbours.
Define one micrometre as one thousandth of a millimetre.
Assess the 7-to-10-micrometre lymphocyte size and the proposed two-cell-width interpretation of a 20-micrometre radius; do not equate proximity with contact.
Preserve the processing pipeline and analyst choices, while qualifying the diagram's claim that every metric yields one number per region or slide.
Explain why tumour-versus-stromal location matters for contact-dependent T-cell killing without inferring killing from a map.

Verify Elomaa's G-cross example: 983 and independent 246 colorectal-cancer patients, 20-micrometre tumour-to-T-cell scope, cancer-specific survival and adjusted hazard ratios 0.33 (0.20 to 0.52) and 0.15 (0.05 to 0.45), distinct from density.
Verify Gide's melanoma example: 27 anti-PD-1 monotherapy and 34 combination patients, CD8 cells within 20 micrometres and response association.
Verify Maley's breast-cancer colocalisation example on routine slides, 486 and 516 women from separate cohorts, with survival association.
Verify Walker's 1,467-patient CD8 proximity and recurrence-free-survival association compared with CD8 density.
Verify Keren's 41-tumour triple-negative mixed/compartmentalised pattern association and keep it distinct from prospective prediction.
Keep group associations separate from a validated individual prognosis or treatment-selection rule.
Assess, rather than silently endorse, the global claim that no locked distance threshold has prospective validation and no distance metric is approved.
Compare standardised compartment-based stromal TIL assessment with distance metrics without assigning all assays a universal validation ranking.
Retain and recompute the fictional counts: 60 of 200 CD8 cells is 30 percent, while 15 of 300 is five percent after moving the region two millimetres.
Explain that a changed analysis region can change the result while the tumour, stain and radius are held fixed in the fictional example.
Require section identity and biopsy-versus-resection context when interpreting a spatial result.
Require cell-defining markers and a check of segmentation and cell calls.
Report whole-slide versus chosen-region scope, the selector and the selection rule.
Report the metric, the cell-type pair, the direction or denominator and any radius.
Separate a threshold fixed before outcome inspection from one fitted to the cohort.
Require independent validation of the same metric definition.
Verify Taube's six-site PD-1/PD-L1 proximity reproducibility example and the reported R-squared of 0.82 with its precise scope.
Distinguish reproducible measurement from outcome prediction or clinical utility.
Explain that cells 15 micrometres apart need not interact and adjacency alone cannot establish T-cell functional state.
Keep the share of T cells near tumour distinct from the share of tumour cells near T cells; reversing the reference population changes the denominator.
Do not transfer a result between 10-, 20- and 30-micrometre radii without checking the changed definition.
Do not treat a cohort-selected cutoff as a clinically validated test.
Verify Lin's two-dimensional-versus-three-dimensional topology caution: apparent separation, contact and connected structures can differ across sections.
Explain how segmentation or signal-spillover errors can create false cell calls and false neighbours.
For a fictional 3.2-times-closer report, require matched region-selection rules, comparable specimen types, a fixed metric and radius, and variation between sections of the block.
Answer the teach-back by separating described spatial closeness from proof of interaction and from an individual patient outcome.
